headline: Nagabiku is 長い (nagai) plus 引く (hiku).
Bō, “pole”, is from Middle Chinese 棒, the goon pronunciation, so likely an earlier borrowing.
Gurasu is English glass, a doublet of ガラス (garasu), from Dutch.
Katsuryoku is 活 (katsu, “life”) plus 力 (-ryoku, “power”).
Shukushō is 縮 (shuku, “shrink,” “reduce,” “shorten”) plus 小 (shō, “small,” “little”).
Joshi is 助 (jo, “helper”) plus 詞 (shi, “word”).
Inki is borrowed from Dutch inkt, ultimately from Ancient Greek énkauston, “burned-in”.
Gutai is Middle Chinese 具體, literally “arrange + body”, repurposed in 1881 as a translation of English concrete.
Tsuru, “to fish”, is cognate with 吊る (tsuru, “to hang”).
Tondemonai is considered a shift from 途でもない (to de mo nai, literally “that is not even the way”).
Sutajio is an internationalism, perhaps from English studio, with its vowel transcribed as a, possibly through confusion with study.
ランプ covers “lamp” and “ramp”: the lamp is from Dutch lamp, later reinforced by English, and the ramp is from English ramp.
Hi, “day”, comes from Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *pi (“day”).
Tabaneru is apparently related to 束 (taba, “bundle”).
Naisho is a sound shift from 内証 (naishō, “a secret”).
ポジション is from English position.
Jishu is from Middle Chinese 自首, literally “self + report to the authorities; plead guilty”, first mentioned in the Ritsuryō legal code of 718 CE.
Samurai is a sound shift from saburai, itself the stem of classical 侍ふ (saburafu, “to serve”).
コントラスト is an internationalism, pointing to English contrast.
In kukaku, 画 is a daiyōji replacing 劃.
セール is from English sale.
ポーズ is from English pause.
Kayu is first attested in the Shoku Nihongi, dated 700, and its derivation beyond that is uncertain.
タワー is from English tower.
Akogare is the continuative stem of the verb 憧れる (akogareru).
Genbun is gen (原, original) plus bun (文, writings).
Kanyū is 加 (ka, “to add”) plus 入 (nyū, “to enter”).
Moshikashite is もし (moshi) plus か (ka) plus して (shite).
Kuchibashi is 口 (kuchi, “mouth”) plus 端 (hashi, “tip; edge”), with hashi voiced to bashi by rendaku.
ドリル is borrowed from English drill.
ミュージック is from English music.
